extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, patent office examiners, judges, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Legal standards and procedural rules governing surrender and reissue of patents, corrections to patents, fees, priority/interference proceedings, and the conclusive effect of the commissioner's decisions under 19th-century U.S. patent law. Focused on when reissue is permitted, limits on amendments, and remedies and defenses in infringement litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commissioner notice and re-examination on rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever, on examination, any claim for a patent is rejected for any reason the commissioner is required to notify the applicant thereof, giving him briefly the reasons for such rejection, together with such information and references as may be useful in judging of the propriety of renewing his application or of altering his specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the applicant, after receiving such notice, persists in his claim for a patent with or without altering his specifications, the commissioner is required to order a re-examination of the case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interference and priority determination (§42, act of 1870)
rubrics_metrics.description: When an application would, in the opinion of the commissioner, interfere with any pending application or with any unexpired patent, he shall give notice to the applicants or applicant and patentee and shall direct the primary examiner to determine the question of priority of invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The commissioner may issue a patent to the party adjudged the prior inventor unless the adverse party appeals from the decision of the primary examiner or the board of examiners-in-chief within such time (not less than twenty days) as the commissioner shall prescribe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fee schedule under the act of 1870
rubrics_metrics.description: The act establishes specified fees for Patent Office proceedings and services (filing, issuing, caveats, reissue applications, disclaimers, extensions, appeals, certified copies, recording assignments, copies of drawings, and design-patent rates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: filing each original application $15; issuance of each original patent $20; filing each caveat $10; reissue application $30; filing each disclaimer $10; application for extension $50 and granting of extension $50; first appeal to examiners-in-chief $10; appeal to commissioner $20; certified copies ten cents per hundred words; recording assignments $1–$3 depending on length; design cases: 3.5 years $10, 7 years $15, 14 years $30; copies of drawings at reasonable cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signatures and correction of clerical mistakes in patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents shall be signed by the Secretary of the Interior and countersigned by the commissioner; the sanction of the Secretary to a correction of a clerical mistake may be given in writing afterwards and the commissioner may correct clerical mistakes without re-signing or resealing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the mistake occurs in the copy and not the enrolment it may be corrected by the commissioner to conform to the original. If a mistake in the enrolled patent is material, the letters cannot operate except on cases arising after the correction; clerical corrections operate back to the original date of the letters except perhaps as to third persons who acquired intervening rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity of acting commissioner's signature on patents
rubrics_metrics.description: A signature to the patent, and a certificate of copies by a person calling himself 'acting commissioner,' is sufficient on its face in controversies between the patentee and third persons, as the law recognizes an acting commissioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where evidence is offered to prove that the 'acting commissioner' who signs a patent was not appointed by the President, it is doubtful whether that evidence is competent in controversies where he is not a party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds and statutory conditions for surrender and reissue
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever any patent is inoperative or invalid by reason of a defective or insufficient specification, or by reason of the patentee claiming more than he had a right to claim as new, if the error arose by inadvertence, accident, or mistake and without fraudulent or deceptive intention, the commissioner shall, on surrender of the patent and payment of the duty required by law, cause a new patent to be issued to the patentee for the unexpired part of the term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The surrender of the old patent takes effect upon the issue of the amended patent; the commissioner may, in his discretion, issue several patents for distinct and separate parts of the thing patented upon demand and payment of the required fee for each reissue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on introducing new matter or annexing later improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: No new matter shall be introduced into the specification on reissue; the earlier statutory authorization to annex additional improvements to an existing patent was repealed (1861), and where additional improvements are desired independent patents must be applied for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exception: when there is neither model nor drawing, amendments may be made upon proof satisfactory to the commissioner that such new matter or amendment was a part of the original invention and was omitted by inadvertence, accident, or mistake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may apply for reissue (inventor vs. assignee)
rubrics_metrics.description: In cases of patents issued and assigned prior to July 8, 1870, the application for reissue may be made by the assignee; but in the case of patents issued or assigned since that date, the application must be made and the specification sworn to by the inventor, if he be living.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This places a formal prerequisite on later-issued/assigned patents requiring inventor involvement in reissue proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and legitimate use of reissue; anti-patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: The object of surrender and reissue is to enable patentees to remedy accidental mistakes in description or claim; reissue is not intended as a vehicle to expand and equivocal claims or to enlarge coverage beyond the original invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have pointedly condemned the practice of surrendering valid patents and obtaining reissues for the purpose of inserting expanded claims; such conduct may indicate fraudulent intent and is disfavored (see Burr v. Duryee).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption that reissue is for the same invention; commissioner duty
rubrics_metrics.description: A reissue is to be presumed to be for the same invention until the contrary is shown; the commissioner has the duty to see that a reissue does not cover more than the original invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Variations between original and reissued patents do not necessarily imply a different discovery; the right to surrender and receive another was given to enable a more perfect description when mistakes were committed in the first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible scope of amendments to claims and specifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the defect be in the description or the claim, the patentee may surrender his patent and by an amended specification cure the defect; the patentee may restrict or enlarge his claim so as to give it validity and effectuate his invention, but cannot claim a substantially new and different invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For machine patents the model or drawings may only be amended by each other; if there is no model or drawing, the commissioner may permit amendments only upon satisfactory proof that the omitted matter was part of the original invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclusive character of the commissioner's decision on reissue/extension
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the statutes and cases, the granting of a reissued (or extended) patent by the commissioner is prima facie and often conclusive evidence that the proofs of defect or the statutory prerequisites were regularly furnished and satisfactory; the commissioner is the primary judge of those facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts generally will not re-examine the commissioner's decision except when it is apparent on the face of the patent that he exceeded his authority, or where there is clear repugnancy between old and new patents, or where there is gross fraud or collusion between the commissioner and the patentee. The Supreme Court has ruled that in suits for infringement defendants are not at liberty to question the commissioner's decision in granting reissue or extension on the ground of fraud; such fraud must be impeached in a proceeding had directly for that purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of reissued patent on subsequent litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent so reissued, together with the corrected specification, shall have the same effect and operation in law, on the trial of all actions thereafter arising, as though the same had been originally filed in such corrected form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subject to limitations noted elsewhere (e.g., no new matter, and the possibility of direct proceedings to impeach a patent), courts treat reissued patents as if originally in corrected form for causes subsequently accruing.
